We have the data
```{r}
x=c(8.3, 8.3, 12.1, 12.1, 17, 17, 17, 24.3, 24.3, 24.3, 33.6)
y=c(227, 312, 362, 521, 640, 539, 728, 945, 738, 759, 1263)
```

We can plot this data
```{r}
plot(y~x)
```

We can use the ``linear model'' command lm(y~x) to find the regression line of $y$ on $x$:
```{r}
regress=lm(y~x)
```
This gives us the model
$$
\hat{y}=36.18 x-12.84
$$
```{r}
summary(regress)
```
There is no evidence that the intercept term is not equal to zero ($p$-value is $0.863$), but there is overwhelming evidence that the gradient term is not equal to zero ($p$-value $4.24 \times 10^{-6}$).

We can add the estimated line to our plot as follows:
```{r}
plot(y~x)
abline(lm(y~x))
```

```{r}
residuals(regress)
plot(residuals(regress)~x)
```
The residuals seem fairly random so the regression model is good.

Next we can look at the correlation coefficient
```{r}
cor(x,y)
```
The correlation coefficient is $0.9561852$ so there is a very strong positive association between $x$ and $y$.

```{r}
predict(regress,data.frame(x=26.0),interval="confidence",level=0.95)
predict(regress,data.frame(x=26.0),interval="prediction",level=0.95)
```
### Question 2

```{r}
lift=c(1.9,3.3,1.2,4.2,1.5,2.2,1.0,5.6,1.9,3.8)
visitor=c(15.1,22.6,9.2,37.5,8.9,21.1,5.8,41.0,9.2,32.4)
```

```{r}
cor(lift,visitor)
plot(lift,visitor)
```
The graph shows a strong positive linear association between $x$ and $y$, the
value of $r=0.966$ is close to $1$ so confirms this.

```{r}
lm(visitor~lift)
```

The equation of the least squares line is
$$
\hat{y}=8.273 x -1.725
$$
```{r}
plot(lift,visitor)
abline(lm(visitor~lift))
```

```{r}
plot(residuals(lm(visitor~lift))~fitted.values(lm(visitor~lift)))
```
The plot is fairly random so the regression equation is good.

Capacity is increased by $500$, so as $x$ is measured in thousands this means $x$ increases by $0.5$.
We know that $\hat{y} = 8.273 x – 1.725$
So our new 
$$
\hat{y}_{new} = 8.273(x+0.5) – 1.725
$$
So the increase is
$$
8.273x + 0.5*8.273 – 1.725 – (8.273x – 1.725)=0.5*8.253= 4.127
$$
